If you want flakey, there are two ways to do this depending on what you mean by "flakey".

The first wat is to layer it like a croissant. You flatten out the dough brush on a layer of melted butter, fold over, flatten again, and repeat a few times.

If you want a flakey crust, you brush on egg whites before you put it in the oven.
buttering between the folds - I had not even considered it. Will be giving it a try this week to see how the result varies.

Don't use a lot of butter. Just a thin coating. It prevents the dough from sticking after folding. The effect should be that, after baking, you can pull apart the layers without having to cut them with a knife.

When my mom taught me, she used a fork as well. She used to say her biscuits could never match her mother's, so I started observing my granny.

She always used her hands, and I swear it makes a lot of difference.
Get your (clean) hands into the bowl and squish that butter right into the flour. Cut the butter into smaller pieces if you want less finger strain, but I never bother.

You know it is blended enough when it has the consistency of fine sand.

Add your milk. Butter milk if you prefer. You do not want the dough so wet that it falls apart while kneeding, but dry dough is the enemy of good biscuits. If it is a little to moist, the flour you place on your kneeding surface will take care of it.

Super important: work the dough as little as possible. The more you work it, the denser it will be.

Just plop the dough from the bowl ontonyour floured surface (flour prevents sticking)

Flour your hands well. (put aside the rolling pin if you were using one)

sprinkle flour lightly across the top of the dough to prevent it from sticking to your hands. If you still end up with any dough stuck to your hands, make sure you remove it well away from your dough. Those clumps will leave hard spots in the biscuits.

Pat your ball of dough reasonably flat. Then gently fold the dough over on itself 3 to 4 times without pressing overly much. This creates layers. After the final fold, gently press the dough to the desired thickness if you insist on using a cutter.

Remeber the first commandent of biscuit making: The less you handle the dough the lighter the biscuit.

Now if you want an even moister biscuit, put away the biscuit cutter.

Pinch off about the same amount as you would cut, or a little more. Gently roll into a ball and pat into a similar shape as a cut biscuit. The sides should be smooth and rounded as opposed to the the rough exposed sides of a cut biscuit. My grandmother used to pinch off a hunk, pinch and twist the bottom closed and then give the biscuit a quick pat to each side to gain the correct shape. She was never very worried about making them perfectly round though, because they were going to be crumbled in gravy anyway. She did make them all approximately the same size.

Either way, a smooth (closed) sided biscuit will retain a lot more moisture while baking.

Last but not least, if you are using a biscuit cutter make sure to blow off any excess flour from the bottoms of the biscuiys before placing on the pan. Dry flour will cause the bottoms to harden and brown too quickly.
